claim: Spinal locomotor circuitry is comprised of rhythm generating centers, one for each limb, that are interconnected by local and long-distance propriospinal neurons.
source: Spinal locomotor circuitry is comprised of rhythm generating centers, one for each limb, that are interconnected by local and long-distance propriospinal neurons thought to carry temporal information necessary for interlimb coordination and gait control.
evidence: This is a statement about the structure of spinal locomotor circuitry that is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Long-distance propriospinal neurons are thought to carry temporal information necessary for interlimb coordination and gait control.
source: Spinal locomotor circuitry is comprised of rhythm generating centers, one for each limb, that are interconnected by local and long-distance propriospinal neurons thought to carry temporal information necessary for interlimb coordination and gait control.
evidence: This represents a hypothesis or theoretical understanding about the function of propriospinal neurons.

claim: Conditional silencing of long ascending propriospinal neurons (LAPNs) that project from L1/L2 to C6 disrupts right-left alternation of both forelimbs and hindlimbs without significantly disrupting other fundamental aspects of interlimb and speed-dependent coordination.
source: We showed previously that conditional silencing of the long ascending propriospinal neurons (LAPNs) that project from the lumbar to the cervical rhythmogenic centers (L1/L2 to C6), disrupts right-left alternation of both the forelimbs and hindlimbs without significantly disrupting other fundamental aspects of interlimb and speed-dependent coordination (Pocratsky et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous publication by the authors.

claim: Silencing LAPNs after a moderate thoracic contusive spinal cord injury resulted in better recovered locomotor function.
source: Subsequently, we showed that silencing the LAPNs after a moderate thoracic contusive spinal cord injury (SCI) resulted in better recovered locomotor function (Shepard et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous publication by the authors.

claim: Long descending propriospinal neurons (LDPNs) have cell bodies at C6 and terminals at L2.
source: In this research advance, we focus on the descending equivalent to the LAPNs, the long descending propriospinal neurons (LDPNs) that have cell bodies at C6 and terminals at L2.
evidence: This is an anatomical description of the LDPNs that defines their location.

claim: Conditional silencing of LDPNs in the intact adult rat resulted in disrupted alternation of each limb pair (forelimbs and hindlimbs).
source: We found that conditional silencing of the LDPNs in the intact adult rat resulted in a disrupted alternation of each limb pair (forelimbs and hindlimbs) and after a thoracic contusion SCI significantly improved locomotor function.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study based on experimental data.

claim: Conditional silencing of LDPNs after a thoracic contusion SCI significantly improved locomotor function.
source: We found that conditional silencing of the LDPNs in the intact adult rat resulted in a disrupted alternation of each limb pair (forelimbs and hindlimbs) and after a thoracic contusion SCI significantly improved locomotor function.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study based on experimental data.

claim: LAPNs and LDPNs have similar roles in the exchange of temporal information between the cervical and lumbar rhythm generating centers.
source: These observations lead us to speculate that the LAPNs and LDPNs have similar roles in the exchange of temporal information between the cervical and lumbar rhythm generating centers, but that the partial disruption of the pathway after SCI limits the independent function of the lumbar circuitry.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation based on the observations from the study.

claim: Partial disruption of the LAPN/LDPN pathway after SCI limits the independent function of the lumbar circuitry.
source: These observations lead us to speculate that the LAPNs and LDPNs have similar roles in the exchange of temporal information between the cervical and lumbar rhythm generating centers, but that the partial disruption of the pathway after SCI limits the independent function of the lumbar circuitry.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation based on the observations from the study.

claim: Silencing LAPNs or LDPNs effectively permits or frees-up the lumbar circuitry to function independently.
source: Silencing the LAPNs or LDPNs effectively permits or frees-up the lumbar circuitry to function independently.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Each limb has its own central pattern generator (CPG).
source: It is now believed that each limb has its own CPG, and that the lumbar and cervical pattern generators are interconnected by a propriospinal network comprised of spinal interneurons with axonal projections that interconnect the cervical and lumbar enlargements (Reed et al., 2006; Brockett et al., 2013; Danner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as current belief in the field and is supported by citations.

claim: Lumbar and cervical pattern generators are interconnected by a propriospinal network comprised of spinal interneurons with axonal projections that interconnect the cervical and lumbar enlargements.
source: It is now believed that each limb has its own CPG, and that the lumbar and cervical pattern generators are interconnected by a propriospinal network comprised of spinal interneurons with axonal projections that interconnect the cervical and lumbar enlargements (Reed et al., 2006; Brockett et al., 2013; Danner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as current belief in the field and is supported by citations.

claim: LAPNs and LDPNs provide functional coupling of the cervical and lumbar enlargements allowing precise temporal information to pass between and among the hindlimb and forelimb CPGs.
source: More specifically, LAPNs and LDPNs provide functional coupling of the two enlargements allowing precise temporal information to pass between and among the hindlimb and forelimb CPGs (Giovanelli Barilari and Kuypers, 1969; Miller et al., 1975; English, 1979; Rossignol et al., 1993; Juvin et al., 2005; Juvin et al., 2012; Pocratsky et al., 2017; Shepard et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The intraspinal network is important for the propagation/integration of supraspinal signals.
source: This intraspinal network is also thought to be important for the propagation/integration of supraspinal signals (Courtine et al., 2008) and sensory information (Alstermark and Isa, 2012) in the uninjured system.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: The intraspinal network is important for the propagation/integration of sensory information in the uninjured system.
source: This intraspinal network is also thought to be important for the propagation/integration of supraspinal signals (Courtine et al., 2008) and sensory information (Alstermark and Isa, 2012) in the uninjured system.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: LDPNs have potential involvement in coordinated patterned behaviors such as locomotion.
source: The LDPNs, a large subset of the spinal inter-enlargement circuitry with cell bodies in the cervical enlargement and projections to the lumbar enlargement, are the current subject of anatomical and molecular investigation due to their potential involvement in coordinated patterned behaviors such as locomotion (Flynn et al., 2017; Reed et al., 2006; Brockett et al., 2013; Ni et al., 2014), as well as their potential for promoting functional recovery from SCI via formation of a de novo bridge to bypass the lesion epicenter (Bareyre et al., 2004; Vavrek et al., 2006; Flynn et al., 2011; Filli et al., 2014; Benthall et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: LDPNs have potential for promoting functional recovery from SCI via formation of a de novo bridge to bypass the lesion epicenter.
source: The LDPNs, a large subset of the spinal inter-enlargement circuitry with cell bodies in the cervical enlargement and projections to the lumbar enlargement, are the current subject of anatomical and molecular investigation due to their potential involvement in coordinated patterned behaviors such as locomotion (Flynn et al., 2017; Reed et al., 2006; Brockett et al., 2013; Ni et al., 2014), as well as their potential for promoting functional recovery from SCI via formation of a de novo bridge to bypass the lesion epicenter (Bareyre et al., 2004; Vavrek et al., 2006; Flynn et al., 2011; Filli et al., 2014; Benthall et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: SCI disrupts the communication between the brain and spinal cord, resulting in an immediate inability to initiate and maintain patterned weight-supported locomotion at or below the level of lesion.
source: SCI disrupts the communication between the brain and spinal cord, resulting in an immediate inability to initiate and maintain patterned weight-supported locomotion at or below the level of lesion (Dietz and Harkema, 2004; Fong et al., 2009; Côté et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about SCI supported by citations.

claim: Most clinical SCIs are anatomically incomplete as there is some sparing of white matter at the lesion epicenter, most often the outermost rim of the lateral and ventrolateral funiculi where the LAPN and LDPN axons reside.
source: Even if classified as neurologically complete, most clinical SCIs are anatomically incomplete as there is some sparing of white matter at the lesion epicenter, most often the outermost rim of the lateral and ventrolateral funiculi where the LAPN and LDPN axons reside.
evidence: This is a statement about the typical anatomy of clinical SCIs.

claim: LAPN and LDPN axons may comprise a percentage of the anatomically spared circuitry after SCI, thus providing a functional bridge across the injury site.
source: Therefore, these neurons and their axons may comprise a percentage of the anatomically spared circuitry, thus providing a functional bridge across the injury site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical location of these neurons.

claim: LAPNs and LDPNs are well-suited to participate in locomotor recovery after incomplete SCI due to their anatomical characteristics, resistance to cell death following incomplete SCI, and presumed function in intact animals.
source: Due to these anatomical characteristics, their resistance to cell death following incomplete SCI, and their presumed function in intact animals, these neurons are well-suited to participate in locomotor recovery after incomplete SCI (Conta and Stelzner, 2004; Conta Steencken and Stelzner, 2010; Conta Steencken et al., 2011; Siebert et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple characteristics and is supported by citations.

claim: LAPNs secure left-right coordination of the hindlimbs and forelimbs in a context-dependent manner during locomotion.
source: Our recently published work which targeted LAPNs before and after a low thoracic contusive SCI revealed that the LAPNs secure left-right coordination of the hindlimbs and forelimbs in a context-dependent manner during locomotion (Pocratsky et al., 2020; Shepard et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications by the authors.

claim: When LAPNs were silenced, animals displayed right-left coordination (phase values) outside of alternation at speeds normally associated with strict alternation and without disruption of the primary speed-dependent gait characteristics.
source: More explicitly, when LAPNs were silenced, animals displayed right-left coordination (phase values) outside of alternation (values ~0.5), but at speeds normally associated with strict alternation and without disruption of the primary speed-dependent gait characteristics (e.g. stance/swing times).
evidence: This is a description of experimental findings from previous work.

claim: The LAPN silencing phenotype was context-specific and only occurred when animals were moving from point A to B, nose up on a surface with a high coefficient of friction.
source: This phenotype was context-specific and only occurred when the animals were moving from point A to B, nose up on a surface with a high coefficient of friction.
evidence: This is a description of experimental findings from previous work.

claim: The LAPN silencing phenotype disappeared when animals explored (nose-down), when on a low coefficient of friction surface, or when on a treadmill.
source: The phenotype disappeared (strict alternation was observed) when animals explored (nose-down), when on a low coefficient of friction surface, or when on a treadmill.
evidence: This is a description of experimental findings from previous work.

claim: LAPNs have a maladaptive role in recovered locomotion after SCI.
source: Silencing LAPNs restored overground stepping ability, suggesting LAPNs have a maladaptive role in recovered locomotion after SCI (Shepard et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental findings supported by citation.

claim: Some LDPNs are spared post-SCI and could serve as a neural substrate for functional recovery.
source: As described earlier, the anatomical location of LDPNs suggests some are spared post-SCI and could serve as a neural substrate for functional recovery (Reed et al., 2006; Brockett et al., 2013; Pocratsky et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on anatomical location and supported by citations.

claim: Silencing LDPNs in the intact animal resulted in disrupted alternation of the hindlimb and forelimb pairs.
source: When the LDPNs were silenced in otherwise intact animals, we observed a disruption of right-left hindlimb and forelimb alternation that was, in many respects, similar to those observed for LAPN silencing.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study based on experimental data.

claim: LDPN silencing showed a substantial proportion of irregular steps with a bias towards the hindlimbs.
source: The two limb pairs demonstrated a substantial proportion of irregular steps and the disruption involved a similar bias towards the hindlimbs, with the forelimb pair showing less significant disruption (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: LDPN silencing disrupted left-right hindlimb alternation for both the hindlimbs and forelimbs on both low and high coefficient of friction surfaces.
source: However, in contrast to the highly context-dependent LAPN phenotype, LDPN silencing disrupted left-right hindlimb alternation for both the hindlimbs and forelimbs and occurred on both the low CoF (Figure 2a–c; small yellow circles; Videos 1 and 2) and the high CoF (Figure 2A, D and E; small red circles; Videos 3 and 4) surfaces.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study based on experimental data shown in figures and videos.

claim: A second round of Dox administration led to greater disruptions in the alternation of both limb pairs during LDPN silencing.
source: Also distinct from what we saw with the LAPNs, a second round of Dox administration led to greater disruptions in the alternation of both limb pairs, as well as the contralateral hindlimb-forelimb pair, such that there were a greater number of irregular steps during Dox2 than during Dox1, and again these disruptions occurred on both surfaces (Figure 2B–E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Pocratsky et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study based on experimental data shown in figures.

claim: During LDPN silencing, there were modest but significant changes in heterolateral/contralateral and homolateral/ipsilateral forelimb-hindlimb coupling.
source: During silencing, the disruption to interlimb coordination included modest but significant changes in heterolateral/contralateral and homolateral/ipsilateral forelimb-hindlimb coupling, as observed previously when silencing the LAPNs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Pocratsky et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study based on experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The disruption of forelimb-hindlimb coupling is secondary to the partial de-coupling of the forelimb and hindlimb pairs.
source: Based on the magnitude of the effect and the apparent hierarchy of impact, we consider the disruption of forelimb-hindlimb coupling to be secondary to the partial de-coupling of the forelimb and hindlimb pairs (see discussion).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The silencing effects on limb pair relationships were restored when Dox was removed from the drinking water.
source: The silencing effects on limb pair relationships were restored when Dox was removed from the drinking water (Figure 2B–E, 'PostD1').
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study based on experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Silencing LDPNs did not affect the fundamental gait relationships of swing, stance, or stride times regardless of walking surface.
source: As observed previously for the LAPNs, silencing LDPNs did not affect the fundamental gait relationships of swing, stance, or stride times regardless of walking surface (Figure 3A–C and F–H).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study based on experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Stride distance and frequency were unaffected by LDPN silencing.
source: Stride distance and frequency were also unaffected (Figure 3D, E, I and J).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study based on experimental data shown in figures.

claim: LDPN animals exhibited greater variability in many outcome measures compared to LAPN animals, even at control time points.
source: It is interesting to note that overall, even at control time points, the LDPN animals exhibited greater variability in many of the outcome measures, as compared to the LAPNs, but both groups showed a small, but statistically significant increase in mean speed during silencing regardless of stepping surface (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study based on experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Both LAPN and LDPN silenced groups showed a small, but statistically significant increase in mean speed during silencing regardless of stepping surface.
source: It is interesting to note that overall, even at control time points, the LDPN animals exhibited greater variability in many of the outcome measures, as compared to the LAPNs, but both groups showed a small, but statistically significant increase in mean speed during silencing regardless of stepping surface (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study based on experimental data shown in figures.

claim: LAPNs and LDPNs have roles in securing interlimb coordination but removing them from the circuitry does not affect velocity-dependent step cycle characteristics or the locomotor rhythm in an otherwise intact rat.
source: Thus, these findings suggest that both the LAPNs and LDPNs have roles in securing interlimb coordination but that removing them from the circuitry does not affect velocity-dependent step cycle characteristics or the locomotor rhythm in an otherwise intact rat.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Silencing LDPNs had no effect on left-right hindlimb alternation during swimming.
source: In contrast to our overground findings, and in keeping with our previous LAPN study (Pocratsky et al., 2020), silencing the LDPNs had no effect on left-right hindlimb alternation during swimming (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study based on experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The LDPN locomotor phenotype is not rigidly context-independent.
source: This observation suggests that the LDPN locomotor phenotype is not rigidly context-independent.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the swimming experiment findings.

claim: The circuitry responsible for securing alternation during swimming remains unperturbed when either set of long propriospinal neuron is silenced.
source: Thus, the circuitry responsible for securing alternation during swimming remains unperturbed when either set of long propriospinal neuron is silenced.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the swimming experiment findings.

claim: The average spared white matter percentage amongst all animals was 26%.
source: Amongst all animals, the average spared white matter percentage (SWM%) was 26%, slightly higher than that previously described in the LAPN SCI study (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from histological analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The proposed location of LDPN axons within the VLF was spared after SCI.
source: The proposed location of LDPN axons within the VLF was spared, as evidenced by the remaining spared white matter in each animal (Figure 5B–I).
evidence: This is a finding from histological analysis shown in Figures 5B-I.

claim: A proportion of LDPN axons are likely spared after SCI.
source: Thus, a proportion of LDPN axons are likely spared after SCI, a critical finding for the interpretation of any behavioral assessments moving forward.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the histological findings.

claim: Putatively positive eTeNT.EGFP fibers were found to surround neuronal processes in the rostral lumbar enlargement.
source: Histological analysis for EGFP immunoreactivity showed that putatively positive eTeNT.EGFP fibers were found to surround neuronal processes in the rostral lumbar enlargement (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: eTeNT.EGFP co-localized with synaptophysin (synaptic marker).
source: eTeNT.EGFP co-localized with synaptophysin (Figure 6B; synaptic marker), vesicular GABA transporter (Figure 6D, VGAT, inhibitory neurotransmitter), and vesicular glutamate transporter 1/2 (Figure 6E; VGlut2, excitatory neurotransmitters).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: eTeNT.EGFP co-localized with vesicular GABA transporter (VGAT, inhibitory neurotransmitter).
source: eTeNT.EGFP co-localized with synaptophysin (Figure 6B; synaptic marker), vesicular GABA transporter (Figure 6D, VGAT, inhibitory neurotransmitter), and vesicular glutamate transporter 1/2 (Figure 6E; VGlut2, excitatory neurotransmitters).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: eTeNT.EGFP co-localized with vesicular glutamate transporter 1/2 (VGlut2, excitatory neurotransmitters).
source: eTeNT.EGFP co-localized with synaptophysin (Figure 6B; synaptic marker), vesicular GABA transporter (Figure 6D, VGAT, inhibitory neurotransmitter), and vesicular glutamate transporter 1/2 (Figure 6E; VGlut2, excitatory neurotransmitters).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Putatively eTeNT-EGFP-positive LDPN cell bodies co-localized with fluorescent Nissl stained neurons in the intermediate gray matter.
source: Putatively eTeNT-EGFP-positive LDPN cell bodies co-localized with fluorescent Nissl stained (NeuroTrace) neurons in the intermediate gray matter (Figure 6f–H, Reed et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figures 6F-H.

claim: Double-infected LDPNs maintained expression of eTeNT at the level of both the cell soma and axon terminals following SCI.
source: Taken together with the lumbar spinal cord histology, these data suggest that double-infected LDPNs maintained expression of eTeNT at the level of both the cell soma and axon terminals following SCI.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunohistochemical findings.

claim: Any post-SCI spared LDPNs axons were functionally silenced during Dox administration.
source: Furthermore, any post-SCI spared LDPNs axons were functionally silenced, indicating that any behavioral changes seen during Dox administration were concomitant with active eTeNT.EGFP expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the histological and behavioral findings.

claim: Control BBB scores (post-injury, pre-silencing) were concentrated around a score of 12.
source: Control BBB scores (post-injury, pre-silencing) were concentrated around a score of 12, consistent with previous literature for this injury severity and with our previous LAPN silencing study (Shepard et al., 2021; Basso et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral assessment data that is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Average BBB scores were modestly increased during LDPN silencing post-SCI.
source: Analogous to our LAPN study, average BBB scores were modestly increased during silencing (Figure 7A), with a greater proportion of raw scores for each limb between 13–18 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from behavioral assessment data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: The increased BBB scores during LDPN silencing were due to improved weight support of the hindlimbs as well as better 'coordination'.
source: The increased BBB scores were due to improved weight support of the hindlimbs as well as better 'coordination,' resulting in the appearance of improved stepping during silencing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the BBB score findings.

claim: RI and CPI were both modestly improved during Dox administration post-SCI.
source: RI and CPI were both modestly improved during Dox administration (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from behavioral assessment data shown in Figures 7C and 7D.

claim: PSI was modestly improved during LDPN silencing post-SCI.
source: We also examined the plantar stepping index (PSI), an index that simply compares the number of hindlimb plantar steps as compared to forelimb plantar steps, and it was also modestly improved during silencing (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from behavioral assessment data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The DSI was significantly reduced from 24.31±21.02 to 9.64±8.70 during LDPN silencing post-SCI.
source: The DSI was significantly reduced from 24.31±21.02–9.64±8.70 during silencing indicating a significant reduction in the overall proportion of dorsal steps (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from behavioral assessment data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The decrease in DSI during LDPN silencing closely resembles the decrease seen in dorsal stepping indices during LAPN post-SCI silencing.
source: This decrease closely resembles the decrease seen in dorsal stepping indices during LAPN post-SCI silencing.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous findings from LAPN silencing studies.

claim: The sidedness of dorsal steps did not change between control and silencing, with ~55% of dorsal steps occurring in the right hindlimb and ~45% occurring in the left hindlimb.
source: The sidedness did not change between control and silencing, with ~55% of dorsal steps occurring in the right hindlimb and ~45% of dorsal steps occurring in the left hindlimb during both control and silenced time points (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is a primary finding from behavioral assessment data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: One limb did not improve to a greater extent than the other during LDPN silencing post-SCI.
source: This is an important observation, as it shows that one limb did not improve to a greater extent than the other.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the dorsal step sidedness findings.

claim: The excursions of both the distal and proximal angles were not significantly improved during LDPN silencing post-SCI.
source: Interestingly, the excursions of both the distal and proximal angles were not significantly improved during silencing (Figure 8E and F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from kinematic analysis shown in Figures 8E and 8F.

claim: The average coordination value of the proximal and distal angles was unchanged between Control and Dox post-SCI, even while the variability was somewhat reduced.
source: Following injury, the average coordination value of these two angles was unchanged between Control and Dox, even while the variability was somewhat reduced (Figure 8G), indicating that silencing the LDPNs had a negligible effect on intralimb coordination post-SCI.
evidence: This is a primary finding from kinematic analysis shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Silencing the LDPNs had a negligible effect on intralimb coordination post-SCI.
source: Following injury, the average coordination value of these two angles was unchanged between Control and Dox, even while the variability was somewhat reduced (Figure 8G), indicating that silencing the LDPNs had a negligible effect on intralimb coordination post-SCI.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kinematic analysis findings.

claim: The coupling of the hindlimbs was significantly restored during the initial round of post-injury LDPN silencing (D2D5 & D2D8).
source: We found that the coupling of the hindlimbs was significantly restored during the initial round of post-injury silencing (D2D5 & D2D8).
evidence: This is a primary finding from interlimb coordination analysis.

claim: Heterolateral coupling (HL-FL) was improved during LDPN silencing post-SCI, but reached significance only on D8.
source: Heterolateral coupling (HL-FL) was also improved, but reached significance only on D8.
evidence: This is a primary finding from interlimb coordination analysis.

claim: The improvement in HL-HL coupling was not significant at any Dox3 time point, suggesting that there may be some plastic changes occurring within the circuitry over the 3 week period from D2D5 to D3D14.
source: Interestingly, the improvement in HL-HL coupling was not significant at any Dox3 time point, suggesting that there may be some plastic changes occurring within the circuitry over this 3 week period from D2D5 to D3D14.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the interlimb coordination findings suggesting plasticity.

claim: Hindlimb coupling is significantly improved when Control and Dox time points are collapsed, with abnormal steps reduced from ~23% to ~12%.
source: Importantly, hindlimb coupling is seen as significantly improved when Control and Dox time points are collapsed, suggesting that the total number of steps that fall outside normal variability are reduced overall by LDPN silencing from ~23 – ~12% (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from interlimb coordination analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The coupling of the heterolateral hindlimb-forelimb pair was significantly improved overall when control and Dox time points were collapsed, with abnormal steps reduced from ~43% to ~37%.
source: In addition, the coupling of the heterolateral hindlimb-forelimb pair was also significantly improved overall, when the control and Dox time points were collapsed (Figure 9B), even though the absolute reduction in abnormal steps was modest (from ~43 – ~37%; Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from interlimb coordination analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Forelimb-forelimb alternation was maintained during both control and Dox time points post-SCI.
source: Finally, forelimb-forelimb alternation was maintained during both control and Dox time points (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from interlimb coordination analysis shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Post-injury silencing significantly improved hindlimb-hindlimb alternation, had only a modest effect on the hindlimb-forelimb relationship and no impact on right-left forelimb coordination.
source: To summarize the findings on interlimb coordination, post-injury silencing significantly improved hindlimb-hindlimb alternation, had only a modest effect on the hindlimb-forelimb relationship and no impact on right-left forelimb coordination, which remained alternating throughout after injury.
evidence: This is a summary of the interlimb coordination findings.

claim: The injury eliminated the impact of LDPN silencing on forelimb circuitry even though the cell bodies of the neurons being silenced are rostral to the injury.
source: Thus, the injury eliminated the impact of LDPN silencing on forelimb circuitry even though the cell bodies of the neurons being silenced are rostral to the injury.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the post-injury findings.

claim: Silencing the LAPNs after injury improved the interlimb coordination (alternation) of the hindlimbs with essentially no impact on homo- or heterolateral interlimb (HL-FL) coupling.
source: In contrast, in our previous work, we showed that silencing the LAPNs after injury improved the interlimb coordination (alternation) of the hindlimbs with essentially no impact on homo- or heterolateral interlimb (HL-FL) coupling (Shepard et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous findings from LAPN silencing studies.

claim: The reduced prevalence of dorsal steps during post-injury silencing of both LAPNs and LDPNs accounted for some, but not all, of the improvement in hindlimb interlimb coordination.
source: Finally, the reduced prevalence of dorsal steps during post-injury silencing of both LAPNs and LDPNs accounted for some, but not all, of the improvement in hindlimb interlimb coordination.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings comparing dorsal steps to coordination improvements.

claim: Gait angle was modestly improved during LDPN silencing post-SCI.
source: Thus, we looked at gait angle, the angle made by three subsequent hindlimb placement points (R-L-R), diagonal length (distance from L hindpaw to R forepaw placement), and rear track width (distance between R and L hindpaw placements) and found that all three were modestly improved during silencing (Figure 10A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from postural stability analysis shown in Figures 10A-C.

claim: Diagonal length was modestly improved during LDPN silencing post-SCI.
source: Thus, we looked at gait angle, the angle made by three subsequent hindlimb placement points (R-L-R), diagonal length (distance from L hindpaw to R forepaw placement), and rear track width (distance between R and L hindpaw placements) and found that all three were modestly improved during silencing (Figure 10A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from postural stability analysis shown in Figures 10A-C.

claim: Rear track width was modestly improved during LDPN silencing post-SCI.
source: Thus, we looked at gait angle, the angle made by three subsequent hindlimb placement points (R-L-R), diagonal length (distance from L hindpaw to R forepaw placement), and rear track width (distance between R and L hindpaw placements) and found that all three were modestly improved during silencing (Figure 10A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from postural stability analysis shown in Figures 10A-C.

claim: The number of foot slips on the ladder apparatus was reduced for both the left and right hindlimbs during post-injury LDPN silencing.
source: The number of foot slips, or times that the foot doesn't maintain contact with a rung, was reduced for both the left and right hindlimbs (Figure 10D) during post-injury LDPN silencing.
evidence: This is a primary finding from ladder task analysis shown in Figure 10D.

claim: Silencing LDPNs restored the relationships between speed and spatiotemporal features of limb movements post-SCI and resulted in a dramatic reduction in the variability of abnormal steps.
source: Silencing LDPNs restored these relationships and resulted in a dramatic reduction in the variability of abnormal steps, regardless of dorsal or plantar stepping (Figure 11F–J).
evidence: This is a primary finding from spatiotemporal analysis shown in Figures 11F-J.

claim: Average swing and stance times were unchanged during post-SCI LDPN silencing.
source: Importantly, average swing (Figure 11K) and stance times (Figure 11L) were unchanged during post-SCI silencing as was the duty cycle (Figure 11M).
evidence: This is a primary finding from spatiotemporal analysis shown in Figures 11K-M.

claim: The average locomotor speed was modestly increased during post-injury LDPN silencing.
source: Finally, the average locomotor speed was modestly increased during post-injury silencing (Figure 11N) suggesting that speed may be a factor in the improved spatiotemporal relationships.
evidence: This is a primary finding from spatiotemporal analysis shown in Figure 11N.

claim: Speed may be a factor in the improved spatiotemporal relationships during LDPN silencing post-SCI.
source: Finally, the average locomotor speed was modestly increased during post-injury silencing (Figure 11N) suggesting that speed may be a factor in the improved spatiotemporal relationships.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the speed findings.

claim: Silencing LDPNs after SCI positively influences the temporal coordination of multiple aspects of locomotion, primarily interlimb (HL-HL) coordination.
source: Together with the previous findings, these data suggest that silencing LDPNs after SCI positively influences the temporal coordination of multiple aspects of locomotion, primarily interlimb (HL-HL) coordination.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the post-SCI findings.

claim: The overall magnitude of improvement with LDPN silencing post-SCI is modest compared to LAPN silencing, where LAPN silencing induced a more robustly improved phenotype.
source: It is imperative to note that while the pattern of improvements observed with LDPN silencing post-SCI is very similar to those seen when the LAPNs were silenced, the overall magnitude of improvement is modest by comparison, where the LAPN silencing induced a more robustly improved phenotype.
evidence: This is a comparison of the magnitude of effects between LDPN and LAPN silencing.

claim: Inter-enlargement LDPNs are an essential pathway in securing interlimb coordination of both the forelimb and hindlimb pairs.
source: Considerable evidence suggests that LDPNs play a role in interlimb coordination in uninjured animals (Matsushita et al., 1979; Skinner et al., 1980; Menétrey et al., 1985; Alstermark et al., 1987; Nathan et al., 1996). Supporting those data, current results indicate that inter-enlargement LDPNs are an essential pathway in securing interlimb coordination of both the forelimb and hindlimb pairs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study's findings and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: When LDPNs were removed from the circuitry via synaptic silencing, there was a greater impact on hindlimb alternation than on the forelimbs.
source: When LDPNs were removed from the circuitry via synaptic silencing, there was a greater impact on hindlimb alternation than on the forelimbs, as shown by the higher proportion of affected steps.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Disrupted forelimb-hindlimb coordination was observed only when the right-left alternation of the forelimb and hindlimb pairs occurred, suggesting that the latter is the primary impact of silencing while the former is a secondary effect.
source: Furthermore, disrupted forelimb-hindlimb coordination was observed only when the right-left alternation of the forelimb and hindlimb pairs occurred, suggesting that the latter is the primary impact of silencing while the former is a secondary effect.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the coordination findings.

claim: Silencing the LDPNs after SCI brought about modest but meaningful improvements in postural stability concomitant with mild but significant improvements in hindlimb-hindlimb coordination.
source: We found that silencing the LDPNs after SCI brought about modest but meaningful improvements in postural stability concomitant with mild but significant improvements in hindlimb-hindlimb coordination, including paw placement order and timing, and speed-dependent gait indices.
evidence: This is a summary of the post-SCI findings.

claim: These improvements occurred in the absence of any disruption to forelimb alternation or changes in hindlimb-forelimb coordination post-SCI.
source: These improvements occurred in the absence of any disruption to forelimb alternation, a hallmark of LDPN silencing in uninjured animals, or changes in hindlimb-forelimb coordination.
evidence: This is a summary of the post-SCI findings.

claim: Rather than securing alternation of the hindlimbs and forelimbs, spared LDPNs hinder the capability of lumbar circuitry below the level of the lesion to function optimally, contributing to diminished stepping capacity at chronic post-injury time points.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that rather than securing alternation of the hindlimbs and forelimbs, spared LDPNs hinder the capability of lumbar circuitry below the level of the lesion to function optimally, contributing to diminished stepping capacity at chronic post-injury time points.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the post-SCI findings.

claim: LAPN silencing in uninjured animals disrupted interlimb coordination that mimicked the findings with LDPN silencing, but with several important differences including more robust perturbations, context-specificity, and more even disruption to both forelimb and hindlimb pairs.
source: LAPN silencing in uninjured animals disrupted interlimb coordination that mimicked the findings with LDPN silencing, but with several important differences. Perturbations with LAPN silencing were more robust, context-specific, and had a more even disruption to both forelimb and hindlimb pairs.
evidence: This is a comparison of LAPN and LDPN silencing effects.

claim: Neither LAPN nor LDPN manipulation significantly influenced interlimb coordination during swimming, intralimb coordination, or speed-dependent gait characteristics during stepping within the limitations of the assessment strategy.
source: Neither manipulation significantly influenced interlimb coordination during swimming, intralimb coordination, or speed-dependent gait characteristics during stepping within the limitations of the assessment strategy.
evidence: This is a summary of findings for both LAPN and LDPN silencing.

claim: LAPNs and LDPNs form an inter-enlargement loop, providing temporal information used to secure R-L coordination within each enlargement.
source: Taken together with our anatomical analysis of these two populations (Pocratsky et al., 2020; Shepard et al., 2021), our results lead us to suggest that LAPNs and LDPNs form an inter-enlargement loop, providing temporal information used to secure R-L coordination within each enlargement.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed based on the findings.

claim: The context specificity of the LAPN-silenced phenotype argues that sensory input is critical, perhaps to trigger enhanced supraspinal oversight when stepping conditions are not optimal.
source: Clearly, the context specificity of the LAPN-silenced phenotype argues that sensory input is critical, perhaps to trigger enhanced supraspinal oversight when stepping conditions are not optimal.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the context-dependent findings.

claim: The speculation that LAPNs and LDPNs are part of an anatomical and functional inter-enlargement network is supported by the similar impact of post-SCI synaptic silencing.
source: The speculation that these two populations are part of an anatomical and functional inter-enlargement network is further supported by the similar impact of post-SCI synaptic silencing.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by the post-SCI findings.

claim: Disruption of an already incomplete ascending-descending circuit frees-up or permits the lumbar spinal circuitry to function more autonomously, unimpeded by incomplete or noisy information.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that disruption of an already incomplete (due to the loss of white matter at the injury epicenter) ascending-descending circuit frees-up or permits the lumbar spinal circuitry to function more autonomously, unimpeded by incomplete or noisy information.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the post-SCI findings.

claim: The thoracic contusion injury resulted in a disruption to hindlimb alternation similar to that seen during LDPN silencing but did not disrupt forelimb alternation.
source: Interestingly, the thoracic contusion injury utilized here and previously (NYU 12.5 g-cm; Shepard et al., 2021) resulted in a disruption to hindlimb alternation similar to that seen during LDPN silencing but did not disrupt forelimb alternation.
evidence: This is a comparison of injury effects to silencing effects.

claim: The loss of the dorsal columns plus some of the LAPN or LDPN axons (following injury) results in an increased supraspinal oversight of forelimb coordination that ignores or is resilient to the additional impact of LAPN or LDPN silencing.
source: This then suggests that the loss of the dorsal columns plus some of the LAPN or LDPN axons (following injury) results in an increased supraspinal oversight of forelimb coordination that ignores or is resilient to the additional impact of LAPN or LDPN silencing.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the post-injury findings.

claim: Forelimb alternation is intact at all time points post-thoracic contusion, whereas hindlimb alternation is disrupted by the thoracic contusion or by LAPN or LDPN silencing.
source: Forelimb alternation is intact at all time points post-thoracic contusion, whereas hindlimb alternation is disrupted by the thoracic contusion or by LAPN or LDPN silencing.
evidence: This is a summary of the post-injury findings.

claim: In the adult mouse, ablation of LDPNs using intersectional approaches reduced the speed and duration of spontaneous locomotor bouts, and disrupted interlimb coordination during high-speed locomotion on a treadmill.
source: Ruder et al., 2016 reported that in the adult mouse, ablation of LDPNs using intersectional approaches reduced the speed and duration of spontaneous locomotor bouts, and disrupted interlimb coordination during high-speed locomotion on a treadmill.
evidence: This is a citation to previous work by Ruder et al., 2016.

claim: Despite the disrupted alternation of the two limb pairs during LDPN silencing, rats are still able to achieve fairly high rates of speed and locomotor bouts are sustained and unperturbed.
source: In contrast, our data indicate that, despite the disrupted alternation of the two limb pairs, rats are still able to achieve fairly high rates of speed and that locomotor bouts are sustained and unperturbed when LDPNs are silenced in otherwise intact adults.
evidence: This is a summary of the current study's findings in contrast to Ruder et al., 2016.

claim: The LDPN population targeted in the current study may be comprised of different sub-populations of long spinal projection neurons that have been previously defined genetically in mice, including V0v and V2a neurons.
source: The LDPN population targeted in the current study may be comprised of different sub-populations of long spinal projection neurons that have been previously defined genetically in mice. Notably, V0v and V2a, but not V0d, neurons residing in the lumbar enlargement have been implicated in securing left-right limb alternation at high speeds (Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015; Crone et al., 2009; Talpalar et al., 2013; Ruder et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the composition of the LDPN population supported by citations.

claim: V0v are composed of commissurally-projecting inhibitory interneurons and are recruited to maintain left-right alternation as the speed of movement increases.
source: V0v are composed of commissurally-projecting inhibitory interneurons and are recruited to maintain left-right alternation as the speed of movement increases (Lanuza et al., 2004; Crone et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about V0v neurons supported by citations.

claim: The V2a population of neurons are classified as ipsilateral excitatory glutamatergic interneurons that are involved in left-right alternation with minimal involvement in rhythm generation.
source: The V2a population of neurons are also classified as ipsilateral excitatory glutamatergic interneurons that are involved in left-right alternation (Crone et al., 2008; Crone et al., 2009) with minimal involvement in rhythm generation.
evidence: This is a statement about V2a neurons supported by citations.

claim: It is likely that the silenced LDPN population includes some proportion of V0v and V2a neurons, given the perturbations to left-right alternation during silencing.
source: It is likely that the silenced LDPN population includes some proportion of each of these defined interneurons, given the perturbations to left-right alternation during silencing.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the functional findings.

claim: LDPNs have characteristics that fall in line with both progenitor domains, as they are both ipsilaterally and commissurally-projecting and co-localize with both glutamatergic and GABAergic synapses.
source: However, it is important to note that LDPNs have characteristics that fall in line with both progenitor domains, as they are both ipsilaterally and commissurally-projecting and co-localize with both glutamatergic and GABAergic synapses.
evidence: This is a statement about the characteristics of LDPNs based on the study's findings.

claim: It is difficult to place anatomically-defined LDPNs within the previously described context of genetically-defined V-neuron classes.
source: Therefore, it is difficult to place these anatomically-defined neurons within the previously described context of genetically-defined V-neuron classes.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the difficulty of classifying LDPNs.

claim: LDPNs are well-suited to receive synaptic contacts from descending supraspinal projections to form 'detour circuits' that might propagate supraspinal motor system commands to below the level of injury.
source: As a consequence of the LDPN cell body position within the cervical spinal cord and their central role in the generation of patterned locomotor output prior to the injury, LDPNs are well-suited to receive synaptic contacts from descending supraspinal projections to form 'detour circuits' that might propagate (i.e. relay) supraspinal motor system commands to below the level of injury (Bareyre et al., 2004; Courtine et al., 2008; Mitchell et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the potential role of LDPNs in recovery supported by citations.

claim: Evidence continues to point to descending propriospinal neurons as potential targets for functional recovery.
source: Consistent with that suggestion, evidence continues to point to these descending propriospinal neurons as potential targets for functional recovery (Taccola et al., 2018; Loy and Bareyre, 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the field's view supported by citations.

claim: The targeted population of LDPNs represents a partially-spared inter-enlargement pathway that should continue to reliably carry information across the level of injury.
source: Our targeted population of LDPNs represents a partially-spared inter-enlargement pathway that should continue to reliably carry information across the level of injury.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the LDPNs based on the study's findings.

claim: Supraspinal motor centers in the cerebellum, cerebral cortex, and brainstem, along with primary afferents, provide monosynaptic input onto LDPN populations in the cervical spinal cord.
source: Early electrophysiological data showed that supraspinal motor centers in the cerebellum, cerebral cortex, and brainstem, along with primary afferents, provide monosynaptic input onto LDPN populations in the cervical spinal cord (Brink et al., 1985; Alstermark et al., 1987).
evidence: This is a statement about LDPN inputs supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Corticospinal and descending serotonergic pathways are present in LDPNs.
source: More recent work has confirmed the presence of corticospinal and descending serotonergic pathways in LDPNs (Ni et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about LDPN inputs supported by citation.

claim: Commissurally-projecting LDPNs received putative synaptic inputs from both excitatory and inhibitory pathways, such as inhibitory pre-motor interneurons, excitatory corticospinal or myelinated afferents, and proprioceptive input from group Ia muscle afferents.
source: Flynn et al., 2017 showed that commissurally-projecting LDPNs received putative synaptic inputs from both excitatory and inhibitory pathways, such as inhibitory pre-motor interneurons, excitatory corticospinal or myelinated afferents, and proprioceptive input from group Ia muscle afferents.
evidence: This is a statement about LDPN inputs supported by citation.

claim: The specific pathways with which inter-enlargement LDPNs interact is not apparent and requires further investigation.
source: Our data showing IHC colocalization with GABA and glutamate (Figure 6) are consistent with those data, but the specific pathways with which inter-enlargement LDPNs interact is not apparent and requires further investigation.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study.

claim: Various populations of descending propriospinal relays of both thoracic and cervical origin are seen as an essential component of recovered stepping ability in several studies.
source: At first glance, our results contradict several studies in the field of locomotor recovery in which various populations of descending propriospinal relays of both thoracic and cervical origin are seen as an essential component of recovered stepping ability (Bareyre et al., 2004; Vavrek et al., 2006; Flynn et al., 2011; Courtine et al., 2008; Courtine et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about previous work in the field supported by citations.

claim: The descending populations in previous studies are inconsistent in terms of their defined anatomy (location of cell bodies and terminals).
source: However, the descending populations in these studies are inconsistent in terms of their defined anatomy (location of cell bodies and terminals, Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a critical observation about the literature.

claim: Even minor differences in the anatomical location of spared pathways may drastically alter their influence on below-level circuitry and their propensity to enhance recovery after SCI.
source: This is a critical consideration, as even minor differences in the anatomical location of spared pathways may drastically alter their influence on below-level circuitry and their propensity to enhance recovery after SCI.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the importance of anatomical specificity.

claim: Descending pathways with more rostral cell bodies within the cervical cord may have an entirely different function than those located more caudally.
source: The extensive differences in how LDPNs are defined may also offer some clues to the described differences in recovered function described here. Descending pathways with more rostral cell bodies within the cervical cord (Bareyre et al., 2004) may have an entirely different function than those located more caudally.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about functional differences based on anatomy.

claim: Whether regeneration/sprouting of supraspinal axons onto LDPNs leads directly to LDPN-dependent improvements in functional outcomes remains uncertain.
source: Some of the referenced studies have also focused specifically on the potential of supraspinal axon regeneration/sprouting and synapse formation onto LDPNs (Vavrek et al., 2006; Courtine et al., 2008). Whether this regeneration/sprouting leads directly to LDPN-dependent improvements in functional outcomes remains uncertain.
evidence: This is a statement about uncertainty in the field.

claim: Spared LDPNs are detrimental to recovered locomotion and thus may not be good targets for regenerative/bridging efforts.
source: Our results suggest that spared LDPNs are detrimental to recovered locomotion and thus may not be good targets for regenerative/bridging efforts.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: Definitive identification of descending propriospinal pathways that do facilitate functional recovery after SCI is essential to understand therapeutically functional plasticity.
source: Definitive identification of descending propriospinal pathways that do facilitate functional recovery after SCI is essential to understand therapeutically functional plasticity.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of future research.
